{{Short description|Point in a convex plane curve where all equal-length chords intersect}}
[[File:Equichordal-center.svg|thumb|Curve (red) with two chords (black), intersecting in the equichordal point.]]
In [[geometry]], an '''equichordal point''' is a point defined relative to a [[Convex set|convex]] plane curve such that all [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] passing through the point are equal in length. Two common figures with equichordal points are the [[circle]] and the [[limaçon]].  It is impossible for a curve to have more than one equichordal point.

==Equichordal curves==
A curve is called equichordal when it has an equichordal point.<ref>{{citation
|author=Steven G. Krantz
|title=Techniques of Problem Solving
|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]
|year=1997
|isbn=978-0-8218-0619-7
}}</ref> Such a curve may be constructed as the [[pedal curve]] of a [[curve of constant width]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Kelly | first = Paul J. | authorlink = Paul Kelly (mathematician)
 | journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | mr = 0092168
 | pages = 333–336
 | title = Curves with a kind of constant width
 | volume = 64
 | year = 1957
 | issue = 5 | doi=10.2307/2309594| jstor = 2309594 }}.</ref> For instance, the pedal curve of a [[circle]] is either another circle (when the center of the circle is the pedal point) or a [[limaçon]]; both are equichordal curves.

==Multiple equichordal points==
{{main|equichordal point problem}}
In 1916 Fujiwara proposed the question of whether a curve could have two equichordal points (offering in the same paper a proof that three or more is impossible). Independently, a year later, Blaschke, Rothe and Weitzenböck posed the same question.<ref>W. Blaschke, W. Rothe, and R. Weitztenböck. Aufgabe 552. Arch. Math. Phys., 27:82, 1917.</ref> The problem remained unsolved until it was finally proven impossible in 1996 by [[Marek Rychlik]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Rychlik | first = Marek
 | doi = 10.1090/S1079-6762-96-00015-7
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Electronic Research Announcements of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1426720
 | pages = 108–123
 | title = The equichordal point problem
 | volume = 2
 | year = 1996| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Rychlik | first = Marek R.
 | doi = 10.1007/s002220050161
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Inventiones Mathematicae
 | mr = 1464869
 | pages = 141–212
 | title = A complete solution to the equichordal point problem of Fujiwara, Blaschke, Rothe and Weitzenböck
 | volume = 129
 | year = 1997| bibcode = 1997InMat.129..141R
 | s2cid = 17998996
 }}.</ref> Despite its elementary formulation, the [[equichordal point problem]] was difficult to solve. [[Rychlik's theorem]] is proved by methods of advanced complex analysis and algebraic geometry and it is 72 pages long.
